title: Revisiting the Veil Nebula
caption: Part of the Veil Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Cygnus Loop, NGC 6960, Veil Nebula · constellation Cygnus · about 2100 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #88 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble zooms in on a small piece of the Veil Nebula, the famous remnant of a supernova. The part pictured lies in the nebula's outer shell, in a region called NGC 6960, or more informally the Witch's Broom Nebula.

A supernova remnant is what is left after a massive star explodes. The blast sends material racing outward, and as it ploughs into the thin gas between the stars, it compresses and heats that gas until it glows. Over time this forms a vast, expanding shell, often laced with delicate filaments, and the Veil is a well-known example.

This view isolates just one piece of that shell, showing it in much finer detail than wide-field views can. Its observations used filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen alongside broader visible and near-infrared filters, which helps separate the glow of different gases.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (7.11 x 4.74 arcminutes) and distance (2100 light years), the frame spans roughly 4.3 × 2.9 light-years. Its light set out about 2,100 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, combining filters for oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen light with broad visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the filaments are far too faint to see in this detail without long exposures.

alt: Glowing filaments of gas in a section of the Veil Nebula.
